question.prompt: For how many integral values of \(x\) can a triangle of positive area be formed having side lengths \(\log_2 x,\) \(\log_4 x,\) and \(3?\)

solutions.title: Use one logarithmic variable
solutions.explanation:
The two logarithmic side lengths have a fixed ratio, so expressing them with one variable makes the triangle inequalities linear.

Positive side lengths require \(x>1\). Let \(t=\log_2 x>0\). By change of base,
\[
\log_4 x=\frac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}=\frac{t}{2},
\]
so the proposed sides are \(t,\frac{t}{2},3\).

For a triangle of positive area, each pair of sides must have sum strictly greater than the remaining side. Two of these inequalities give
\[
t+\frac{t}{2}>3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t>2,
\]
\[
\frac{t}{2}+3>t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t<6.
\]
The third inequality, \(t+3>\frac{t}{2}\), holds automatically for \(t>0\). Conversely, every \(2<t<6\) gives positive sides satisfying all three inequalities.

Because the base-\(2\) logarithm is increasing, the exact condition is
\[
2<\log_2 x<6
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
4<x<64.
\]
The endpoints are excluded because they produce a flat triangle. The allowed integers are \(5,6,\ldots,63\), giving
\[
63-5+1=\boxed{59},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
